title: Antenna patterns and modeling
blurb: Read azimuth and elevation plots for beamwidth, front-to-back and peak angle, and explain far field and Method of Moments modeling.

E9B01.why: The main lobe crosses the −3 dB ring at about 25° each side of the peak. 25° + 25° = **50°** beamwidth.
E9B01.trap: 25° is only half the beamwidth: count both sides.

E9B02.why: Peak is 0 dB at 0°. At 180° the plot is near the −18 ring, so front-to-back = 0 − (−18) = **18 dB**.

E9B03.why: At 90° the side lobe sits near −14 dB. Front-to-side = 0 − (−14) = **14 dB**.
E9B03.trap: 18 dB is the back, not the side: read the ring at 90°, not 180°.

E9B04.why: Peak is 0 dB. At 180° the pattern is about −28 dB, so front-to-back = 0 − (−28) = **28 dB**.

E9B05.why: Angles run from 0° at the horizon to 180° with a ground line below: this half-circle is an **elevation** plot.
E9B05.trap: An azimuth plot is a full circle showing compass direction.

E9B06.why: The longest lobe, the strongest response, points at **7.5°** above the horizon, which is a low takeoff angle.
E9B06.trap: Higher lobes exist but are weaker.

E9B07.why: A lossless antenna can only redirect power. Total radiated power is **the same** as an isotropic radiator's; only its distribution differs.
E9B07.trap: Gain is not extra power, and an isotropic radiator has no 2.15 dB advantage.

E9B08.why: In the far field the **shape of the pattern stops changing with distance**. Only the strength falls.

E9B09.why: **Method of Moments** is the standard way to compute an antenna's currents and pattern in modeling programs.

E9B10.why: Method of Moments splits each wire into short **segments with a uniform current** each, and solves how they interact.
E9B10.trap: It is not a single generator or per-segment voltages.

E9B11.why: Too few segments follow the real current poorly, so the **computed feed point impedance may be incorrect**.
